content: Bacterial oxidation is a bio-hydrometallurgical process specifically designed for the pre-cyanidation treatment of refractory gold ores or concentrates. The bacterial culture used in this process is a mixed consortium consisting of Thiobacillus ferrooxidans, Thiobacillus thiooxidans, and Leptospirillum ferrooxidans. During the bacterial oxidation process, refractory sulfide run-of-mine (ROM) ore or concentrate is brought into contact with the bacterial culture for a defined treatment period under carefully controlled optimal environmental conditions. The bacteria oxidize the sulfide minerals, thereby liberating the encapsulated gold, which can then be recovered through subsequent cyanidation. In a controlled continuous plant setting, the bacterial cell population and their metabolic activity are optimized to achieve the highest possible rate of sulfide oxidation. This is achieved by maintaining a temperature range of 30 to 45°C and ensuring a consistent supply of oxygen and carbon dioxide to support bacterial growth and activity. The unique operating conditions required for these bacteria are not conducive to the growth of most other microorganisms, which eliminates the need for sterility during the process. Organic substances are toxic to these bacteria, rendering them non-pathogenic and incapable of causing disease. As a result, the bacteria used in this process pose no health risks to humans or animals. The bacterial oxidation of iron sulfide minerals results in the production of iron (III) sulfate and sulfuric acid. In the case of arsenopyrite, arsenic acid is also produced. The arsenic is subsequently removed from the solution through co-precipitation with iron and sulfate in a two-stage neutralization process. This process generates a solid neutralization precipitate primarily composed of calcium sulfate, basic iron (III) arsenate, and iron (III) hydroxide. The iron (III) arsenate formed during this process is sufficiently insoluble and stable, allowing the neutralization product to be safely disposed of in a tailings dam. The neutralization liquor, after being purified to contain an acceptable level of arsenic, can be recycled and reused in milling, flotation, or bacterial oxidation circuits.
